questions.q: Define "extended metaphor" and give the two primary tenor-vehicle pairs in "Mother Tongue" without quoting the poem.
questions.a: An extended metaphor sustains a single comparison across multiple lines or stanzas, developing the vehicle's attributes to deepen understanding of the tenor. In this poem: (1) Tenor = Dogri language; Vehicle = Shahni (noblewoman). (2) Tenor = Sharade script; Vehicle = quill cut from the reed's hand. A wrong answer that only identifies "quill = pen" misses the abstraction (script vs. physical object) and reveals the student cannot distinguish literal from metaphorical levels.

questions.q: The poem opens with "I approached a stem / Swinging on a reed." Explain why the poet chooses "stem" and "swinging" instead of "plant" and "growing," and what sensory effect this creates.
questions.a: "Stem" isolates a single, slender, manipulable part (tactile precision) rather than the whole plant; "swinging" adds kinesthetic motion — the reed is alive, responsive, almost human in its gesture. This creates a haptic and dynamic image that prepares the reader for the reed's later personified action (cutting off its hand). A wrong answer focusing only on "visual picture" misses the tactile-kinesthetic layer and shows the student equates imagery solely with sight.

questions.q: In a new context, a student writes: "The constitution is the spine of democracy." Identify the tenor, vehicle, and the specific quality transferred. Then rewrite the sentence as a simile without losing the transferred quality.
questions.a: Tenor = Constitution; Vehicle = spine; Transferred quality = structural support that keeps the body upright and enables movement. Simile rewrite: "The constitution supports democracy like a spine supports a body, keeping it upright and allowing it to move." A wrong answer that says "vehicle = democracy" or transfers "hardness" reveals confusion about directionality (tenor receives qualities from vehicle) and inability to isolate the precise semantic feature.

questions.q: Compare the imagery of the "accountant / With some Shah / Writing account books" (lines 7–9) with the imagery of the reed "cut off its hand / Gave it to me" (lines 15–16). What does the contrast reveal about the poet's view of language?
questions.a: The accountant image is clinical, transactional, repetitive (visual: rows of numbers; tactile: mechanical pen-scratching) — language as bureaucratic tool. The reed's self-amputation is visceral, sacrificial, organic (tactile: severing living tissue; kinesthetic: offering) — language as living entity demanding devotion. The contrast reveals the poet sees her mother tongue not as a utility but as a being worthy of bodily sacrifice. A wrong answer that merely lists images without linking to the poet's stance shows surface-level analysis.

questions.q: Critique this student claim: "The metaphor 'Shahni = mother tongue' fails because a Shahni is a feudal aristocrat, but a mother tongue belongs equally to all speakers." Use evidence from the poem.
questions.a: The claim misreads the metaphor's function: the Shahni's "kindness," "wealth," and "many servants" map onto the language's nurturing capacity, rich expressive resources, and community of poets — not feudal oppression. The poet explicitly says "I am not the only one / Working for her," emphasizing collective service. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim reveals a literalist reading that cannot separate vehicle's cultural connotations from the poet's selective mapping.

questions.q: Write four lines of free verse that extend the "quill = script" metaphor to a modern context (e.g., digital fonts, Unicode, keyboard), maintaining the poem's tone of urgent devotion.
questions.a: Example criteria: (1) Clear tenor (digital script/encoding) and vehicle (keyboard/Unicode/font). (2) At least two sensory images (e.g., "glowing glyphs," "fingertips burning on keys"). (3) Urgency conveyed through imperative or time-pressure diction. (4) Metaphor sustained across all four lines. A poor answer that writes a literal description of typing or uses simile ("like a quill") shows inability to transfer the device creatively.
